title: When Food Aid Shrinks, a San Diego Office Gives Out Groceries
summary:
Early one Saturday morning, Rosa Rodarte went back to her office in San Diego on her day off. She pushed carts of groceries and loaded them into people's cars. Her normal job is helping people sign up for food help. Now she hands out the food itself. 'We want to make sure everybody is helped and not judged,' she says.

The food help is called SNAP, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. It helps people with low incomes buy groceries. About five million people across the country have lost these benefits over the past year, after a big tax and spending law, the One Big Beautiful Bill, was signed in July 2025. The law cut SNAP money, made it harder to qualify, and ended food aid for most asylum seekers and refugees.

In San Diego County, 36,000 fewer people were on SNAP this September than in July 2025. Between August and September, the county and food banks gave out nearly 70,000 pounds of food to more than 5,200 people. New work rules now apply to homeless people, former foster youth, veterans, and parents with a child older than 14.
why_it_matters: This matters because some kids and their families count on food help to eat, and when that help shrinks, free groceries can make a real difference at home.

keywords.explanation: Supplemental means extra help added on top of what someone already has.
Benefits are money or help that the government gives to people who need it.
Asylum seekers are people who ask another country for safety because they are in danger at home.
Refugees are people who have had to leave their home country because it is not safe there.
Foster youth are young people who grew up living with a different family because their own family could not care for them.
Veterans are people who used to serve in the military.
